title: A Computer on One Chip Explained Simply | PUC Electronics Class 11
description:
Aarav opens a broken TV remote and finds no tubes and no tangle of wires, just a flat board and one small chip. How can one chip run everything? In this animated lesson we go from separate parts soldered by hand to Jack Kilby's integrated circuit (1958) and Robert Noyce's mass-produced silicon chips (1959): what an IC contains, why it is called monolithic, the levels of integration (SSI, MSI, LSI, VLSI), and the advantages and limits of ICs.

Then we build a microprocessor block by block (ALU, control unit, registers, buses) and watch the fetch, decode, execute cycle, before memory, input output ports and timers move onto the same chip to make a microcontroller. On a live breadboard a microcontroller blinks a lamp while the program steps line by line and the oscilloscope draws the square wave. We show why n address lines give 2^n addresses, work out that 16 lines reach 64 KB, compare microprocessors and microcontrollers, and finish with the exam trap, where it is asked, an original PUC board pattern practice question with a full solution, and a formula card to screenshot.

This is Episode 3 of PUC Electronics, Class 11, Chapter 1: Introduction to Electronics (Karnataka PUC Electronics).
